comparison: not gradable — a thing either is or isn't; say *completely waterproof*
contrast: *Waterproof* keeps water out completely; *water-resistant* only slows it down, which is what most watches and jackets really are.

senses.gloss: Not letting water through.
examples: These boots are completely *waterproof*.
She keeps her phone in a *waterproof* case.
The jacket looks warm, but it isn't *waterproof*.

senses.gloss: Sealed so tightly that no water can get in or out.
examples: The hatch has a *watertight* seal.
Make sure the container is *watertight* before you ship it.
A submarine is divided into *watertight* compartments.

senses.gloss: Of an argument, a contract or an alibi: impossible to find a hole in.
examples: He has a *watertight* alibi for that night.
The contract is *watertight* — there's no way out of it.
Her case sounded *watertight* to the jury.

senses.gloss: Containing too much water, so that it is thin and weak.
examples: The soup was thin and *watery*.
I don't like *watery* coffee.
The sauce came out more *watery* than I wanted.

senses.gloss: Of eyes: full of tears.
examples: His eyes were red and *watery*.
The onions left me with *watery* eyes.

senses.gloss: Not sure what to decide; changing your mind back and forth.
examples: A few *wavering* senators still hadn't made up their minds.
She gave a *wavering* answer when I asked if she'd stay.
His support for the plan looked *wavering* at best.

senses.gloss: Of a voice, a light or a flame: unsteady, shaking.
examples: A *wavering* voice came from the back of the room.
The candle threw a *wavering* light on the wall.

senses.gloss: With gentle curves, like waves — usually of hair or lines.
examples: She has long *wavy* hair.
The road is marked with *wavy* white lines.
My hair gets *wavier* in humid weather.

senses.gloss: Looking or feeling like wax — smooth, pale and slightly greasy.
examples: The leaves have a thick *waxy* coating.
His skin had turned a pale, *waxy* color.
The cheap chocolate tastes *waxier* than the good kind.

senses.gloss: Hard to control; behaving badly and going your own way.
examples: The school takes in *wayward* teenagers.
Her *wayward* younger brother finally found a job.
He was the most *wayward* of the three sons.

senses.gloss: Of a ball, a shot or a pass: going off in the wrong direction.
examples: A *wayward* pass cost them the game.
The ball took a *wayward* bounce off the wall.

takes: *in* or *at* + noun (a subject you are bad at): *weak in math*, *weak at spelling*
contrast: *Weak* sounds exactly like *week* (неделя). The noun is *weakness*, the verb *weaken*.

senses.gloss: Not physically strong; having little power or energy.
examples: She felt *weak* for days after the flu.
His legs were too *weak* to hold him up.
The patient is getting *weaker*.

senses.gloss: Not strong enough to work well, or likely to break.
examples: The bridge has a *weak* support on the north side.
The Wi-Fi signal is *weak* in the basement.

senses.gloss: Not convincing, or not good enough.
examples: That's a *weak* excuse.
The movie has a *weak* ending.
Math was always my *weakest* subject.

senses.gloss: Of a drink: with too much water in it.
examples: I like my coffee *weak*.
The tea was *weak* and lukewarm.

senses.gloss: Lacking the courage to do what is right or necessary.
examples: The board was too *weak-kneed* to fire him.
Critics called the statement *weak-kneed*.
Don't be *weak-kneed* about it — just say no.

senses.gloss: So shocked, frightened or excited that your legs feel unsteady.
examples: The sight of blood left her *weak-kneed*.
He went *weak-kneed* when she walked into the room.

senses.gloss: Made less strong, less healthy or less powerful than before.
examples: The storm hit a *weakened* levee.
Chemotherapy leaves patients with a *weakened* immune system.
The party came out of the election badly *weakened*.

position: both — almost always before a noun

senses.gloss: Pure enough to be used in a nuclear or chemical weapon.
examples: Inspectors found *weapons-grade* uranium at the site.
The treaty covers *weapons-grade* plutonium.
*Weapons-grade* material is kept under guard.

senses.gloss: Extremely strong or extremely bad — a joking exaggeration.
examples: That's *weapons-grade* nonsense.
The chili at that place is *weapons-grade*.

ru: носибельный, пригодный для носки; носимый (об устройстве)
contrast: The plural noun *wearables* means smartwatches and fitness trackers: *Sales of wearables are up*.

senses.gloss: Comfortable and practical enough to actually wear.
examples: The collection is beautiful but not very *wearable*.
She buys clothes that are *wearable* at the office.
This is the most *wearable* jacket I own.

senses.gloss: Of technology: designed to be worn on the body.
examples: *Wearable* devices track your heart rate all day.
The company makes *wearable* fitness trackers.

takes: *of* + noun or *-ing* (what you have had too much of)
contrast: Don't mix up *weary* WEER-ee (tired) with *wary* WAIR-ee (careful, suspicious): *wary of strangers*, not *weary of strangers*.

senses.gloss: Very tired, especially after long effort.
examples: The hikers came back cold and *weary*.
She gave a *weary* sigh and sat down.
By the third meeting I was *wearier* than ever.

senses.gloss: Tired of something because it has gone on too long.
examples: Voters are *weary* of the same promises.
I'm *weary* of hearing about it.

contrast: A *wearying* trip makes you tired; a *weary* traveler already is tired.

senses.gloss: Making you very tired.
examples: It was a long, *wearying* drive across the state.
The constant arguing is *wearying*.
Nothing is more *wearying* than a day of meetings.

senses.gloss: Rough and worn from years of sun, wind and rain.
examples: A *weather-beaten* barn stood at the edge of the field.
His face was brown and *weather-beaten*.
The sign was so *weather-beaten* you could barely read it.

form: -ed from *weather* (the verb: to change from long exposure)

senses.gloss: Changed in color or texture by long exposure to the weather.
examples: The deck is made of gray *weathered* boards.
*Weathered* rock shows the layers underneath.
The paint on the shutters looked more *weathered* than I remembered.

senses.gloss: Able to stand rain, wind and cold without being damaged.
examples: The speakers are *weatherproof*, so you can leave them outside.
We put a *weatherproof* cover on the grill.
The new windows are fully *weatherproof*.

senses.gloss: With skin joining the toes or fingers, as ducks and frogs have.
examples: Ducks have *webbed* feet.
Frogs push through the water with their *webbed* toes.
The baby was born with slightly *webbed* fingers.

position: both — the 'married' sense before a noun, the 'committed' sense after a verb

senses.gloss: Married — formal or legal language.
examples: Do you take this woman to be your lawfully *wedded* wife?
They celebrated twenty years of *wedded* bliss.
The vows speak of a lawfully *wedded* husband.

senses.gloss: So committed to an idea or a method that you will not give it up.
examples: The mayor is *wedded* to the idea of a new stadium.
She's too *wedded* to her own plan to listen to anyone.

senses.gloss: Stuck tightly in a narrow space, so that it is hard to move.
examples: The car was *wedged* between two trucks.
A coin got *wedged* in the slot.
We sat *wedged* into the back row of the bus.

contrast: *Wee* came from Scotland and sounds folksy in American English. It is mostly kept for two phrases: *a wee bit* (чуть-чуть) and *the wee hours*. For ordinary use say *tiny*.

senses.gloss: Very small — informal and affectionate.
examples: Can I have a *wee* bit of cream in my coffee?
He was just a *wee* boy when they moved here.
She's a *wee* thing — barely five feet tall.

senses.gloss: In *the wee hours*: the very early hours after midnight.
examples: We talked until the *wee* hours of the morning.
The call came in the *wee* hours of Sunday.

senses.gloss: Lasting a week.
examples: They went on a *weeklong* trip to Maine.
The town holds a *weeklong* festival every August.
A *weeklong* strike shut down the port.

contrast: After a verb, *weeping* is the verb, not the adjective: *She was weeping* = она плакала. Only before a noun is it an adjective.

senses.gloss: Crying.
examples: A *weeping* woman sat on the courthouse steps.
*Weeping* relatives waited outside the hospital.

senses.gloss: Of a tree: with long branches that hang down.
examples: There's a *weeping* willow by the pond.
They planted a *weeping* cherry in the front yard.

senses.gloss: Crying easily, or close to tears.
examples: She gets *weepy* at weddings.
I was tired and *weepy* by the end of the day.
The kids get *weepier* the later it gets.

senses.gloss: Of a movie, a song or a book: sentimental and meant to make you cry.
examples: It's a *weepy* holiday movie.
He put on a *weepy* love song and ruined the mood.

takes: *with* or *by* + noun (what the weight or the worry is)
form: past participle of the phrasal verb *weigh down*

senses.gloss: Carrying so much that it is hard to move.
examples: She came in *weighed down* with grocery bags.
The branches were *weighed down* by wet snow.

senses.gloss: Made tired or unhappy by worry, debt or responsibility.
examples: He seemed *weighed down* by guilt.
The company is *weighed down* with debt.

ru: утяжелённый; взвешенный (о среднем); смещённый в чью-то пользу
takes: in the 'unfair' sense, *toward*, *in favor of* or *against* + noun

senses.gloss: Made heavier by adding weight.
examples: She sleeps under a *weighted* blanket.
The base is *weighted* so the lamp won't tip over.

senses.gloss: Counting some parts more than others in a total.
examples: Your final grade is a *weighted* average.
The test is *weighted* toward the last two chapters.

senses.gloss: Arranged so that one side has an advantage.
examples: The rules are *weighted* in favor of landlords.
The whole system is *weighted* against small farms.

senses.gloss: Having no weight, or feeling as if you have none.
examples: Astronauts are *weightless* in orbit.
The fabric is so light it feels *weightless*.
For a second at the top of the hill you feel *weightless*.

senses.gloss: Serious and important; deserving careful thought.
examples: The court has *weighty* matters to decide this term.
He raised a *weightier* question than anyone expected.
There are *weighty* reasons to wait another year.

senses.gloss: Heavy — a formal or literary use.
examples: She carried a *weighty* volume of poetry under her arm.
The package was *weighty* enough to need both hands.

contrast: *Weird* breaks the 'i before e' rule — e-i, not i-e. In casual speech people also say *weird someone out* (to make someone uncomfortable), which is a verb.

senses.gloss: Strange, and hard to explain or get used to.
examples: That's a *weird* thing to say.
It felt *weird* being back in my old school.
The *weirdest* part is that nobody noticed.

takes: *to* + noun (something you may take) or a *to*-infinitive
contrast: *You're welcome* is the standard answer to *thank you*. Keep the adjective apart from the verb: *Guests are welcome* (they are gladly received) but *The host welcomed the guests* (he greeted them).

senses.gloss: Gladly received; making people pleased.
examples: The rain was a *welcome* change after a month of heat.
Your check was a *welcome* surprise.
Nothing is more *welcome* than good news on a Monday.

senses.gloss: Allowed and encouraged to do something or take something.
examples: You're *welcome* to stay for dinner.
Visitors are *welcome* in the garden anytime.

senses.gloss: Friendly to visitors and newcomers; making people feel at home.
examples: The neighbors were warm and *welcoming*.
The lobby has a *welcoming* feel to it.
The church tries hard to be *welcoming* to newcomers.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun (*a well-thought-out plan*); written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Carefully planned, with the details worked out in advance.
examples: It's a *well-thought-out* plan, and cheap to start.
Her essay was *well thought out* and clearly written.
This proposal is *better thought out* than the last one.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Emotionally healthy and able to deal with other people and with life.
examples: They're raising two happy, *well-adjusted* kids.
He seems *well adjusted* after everything he's been through.
Children with a steady routine tend to be *better adjusted*.

ru: поступающий благоразумно; которому лучше бы (сделать что-то)
position: predicative only — almost always *would be well-advised to*
contrast: This is a polite, formal way of saying *should*: *You'd be well-advised to call first* = вам лучше бы позвонить заранее. Its opposite *ill-advised* does go before a noun: *an ill-advised email*.

senses.gloss: Sensible or wise to do something.
examples: You'd be *well-advised* to read the contract first.
Drivers would be *well-advised* to avoid the bridge today.
She'd be *well-advised* to say nothing until the hearing.

comparison: irregular — *better appointed*, *best appointed*; hyphenated before a noun *best-appointed*
form: compound — *well* + *appointed*, here in the old sense 'furnished, equipped'

senses.gloss: Of a room, house or hotel: well furnished and fully equipped — formal.
examples: They stayed in a *well-appointed* suite overlooking the park.
The house is *well-appointed*, with a wine cellar and a gym.
It's the *best-appointed* hotel in town.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Containing the right mix of different things.
examples: Kids need a *well-balanced* diet.
The team is *well balanced* on offense and defense.
This year's roster is *better balanced* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Of a person: calm, sensible and emotionally steady.
examples: She's a *well-balanced* person who doesn't panic.
He came across as calm and *well balanced* in the interview.

contrast: About people, *well-bred* now sounds old-fashioned and a little snobbish; say *polite* or *well-mannered* instead. About animals it is ordinary.

senses.gloss: Polite and well brought up — an older, upper-class word.
examples: He's a *well-bred* young man who writes thank-you notes.
It wouldn't be *well-bred* to ask what it cost.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: from good breeding stock.
examples: The farm sells *well-bred* quarter horses.
Her dogs are *better bred* than most of the ones at the show.

senses.gloss: Picked carefully, and exactly right for the purpose.
examples: She thanked them in a few *well-chosen* words.
The gift was *well chosen*.
His examples could have been *better chosen*.

ru: со связями; с хорошим транспортным сообщением
position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Knowing many important or useful people.
examples: Her father is *well-connected* in Washington.
You need a *well-connected* lawyer for this.
He's *better connected* than anyone else on the committee.

senses.gloss: Of a place: easy to reach by road, rail or flights.
examples: The neighborhood is *well connected* by bus and rail.
They chose a *well-connected* airport hub.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Clear and easy to understand, with the limits spelled out.
examples: Each job here has a *well-defined* set of duties.
The goals need to be *better defined* before we start.
The role of the committee is *well defined* in the bylaws.

senses.gloss: With a clear, sharp shape or edge.
examples: The border is *well defined* along the river.
He has *well-defined* shoulders from years of swimming.

comparison: not gradable — of meat the scale is *rare*, *medium rare*, *medium*, *medium well*, *well-done*; in the 'done skillfully' sense *better done*, *best done*
contrast: *Well done!* on its own is praise — молодец! As a cooking word, *well-done* meat has no pink left in it.

senses.gloss: Of meat: cooked all the way through, with no pink inside.
examples: He orders his steak *well-done*.
The burgers came out *well done*, almost burnt.
How do you like your steak — rare or *well-done*?

senses.gloss: Made or carried out skillfully.
examples: It's a *well-done* documentary about the flood.
The repair was *well done* and cost almost nothing.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Having had a good, usually long education.
examples: She comes from a *well-educated* family.
The workforce in this county is *well educated*.
Today's students are *better educated* than their grandparents were.

contrast: Said of a person's body, *well-endowed* is a joking euphemism for large breasts or genitals — keep it for schools, museums and natural resources.

senses.gloss: Having plenty of money or natural resources.
examples: The university is *well-endowed* and can pay for the scholarships.
The region is *well endowed* with coal and timber.
Private colleges are usually *better endowed* than state schools.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Getting plenty of good food.
examples: The horses looked healthy and *well-fed*.
A *well-fed* crowd left the church basement happy.
Children today are *better fed* than they were a century ago.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Based on good reasons or real facts.
examples: Their fears turned out to be *well-founded*.
He had a *well-founded* suspicion that he was being followed.
My worries were *better founded* than his.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Clean, neat and carefully looked after — of a person's hair and clothes, or of an animal.
examples: A *well-groomed* man in a gray suit answered the door.
Her dog is always *well groomed*.
He's *better groomed* now than he was in college.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Based on solid facts or evidence.
examples: The complaint is *well-grounded*.
Her objection was *well grounded* in the data.

senses.gloss: Having a solid basic knowledge of a subject.
examples: He's *well-grounded* in statistics.
Students should be *well grounded* in the basics before they specialize.
She's *better grounded* in the theory than the rest of us.

senses.gloss: Having plenty of money.
examples: The gallery attracts a *well-heeled* crowd.
*Well-heeled* tourists fill the resort every July.
Her clients are the most *well-heeled* people in the city.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
comparison: irregular — *better informed*, *best informed*; hyphenated before a noun *best-informed*

senses.gloss: Knowing a lot about a subject or about what is going on.
examples: She's a *well-informed* reader of the business press.
Voters need to be *well informed* about the issues.
He's the *best-informed* person in the room.

ru: с благими намерениями, из лучших побуждений
contrast: It almost always comes with a *but*: the intention was good, the result was not. *Well-meaning* says the same thing about a person.

senses.gloss: Meaning to do good, even when the result is not good.
examples: It was a *well-intentioned* rule that made everything slower.
*Well-intentioned* advice can still hurt.
His comment was *well-intentioned* but clumsy.

ru: ухоженный, содержащийся в порядке; тщательно хранимый (о секрете)
position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
comparison: irregular — *better kept*, *best kept*; hyphenated before a noun *best-kept*

senses.gloss: Looked after carefully; neat and in good condition.
examples: They live in a *well-kept* house with a big yard.
The gardens are *well kept* all year.
The trails are *better kept* on the north side of the park.

senses.gloss: Of a secret: successfully kept from other people.
examples: That bakery is the city's *best-kept* secret.
Their engagement was a *well-kept* secret for months.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Built carefully and out of good materials.
examples: It's an expensive coat, but it's *well-made*.
The furniture is simple and *well made*.
These boots are *better made* than the pair I had before.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Polite, with good manners.
examples: Their son is quiet and *well-mannered*.
A *well-mannered* guest writes a thank-you note.
The dogs are surprisingly *well mannered* around small kids.

contrast: *Well-meaning* describes the person; *well-meant* describes what was said or done: *a well-meaning friend* gave me some *well-meant* advice.

senses.gloss: Wanting to help, even when the help does not work.
examples: A *well-meaning* neighbor kept bringing casseroles.
*Well-meaning* people gave us a lot of bad advice.
He's *well-meaning*, just disorganized.

senses.gloss: Of words or an act: intended kindly, though it may not have helped.
examples: The advice was *well-meant* but useless.
Her *well-meant* remark only made things worse.
I know it was *well-meant*, so I said thank you.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
comparison: irregular — *better preserved*, *best preserved*; hyphenated before a noun *best-preserved*

senses.gloss: Still in good condition after a long time.
examples: The town has a *well-preserved* 18th-century church.
The fossil is remarkably *well preserved*.
It's the *best-preserved* Roman theater in the country.

senses.gloss: Of an older person: still looking young — often said jokingly.
examples: He's seventy and very *well-preserved*.
She's *well preserved* for someone who has worked outdoors all her life.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
comparison: irregular — *better qualified*, *best qualified*; hyphenated before a noun *best-qualified*

senses.gloss: Having the training and experience that a job needs.
examples: We had four *well-qualified* candidates for the opening.
She's *well qualified* for the position.
He was the *best-qualified* applicant by far.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
takes: *in* + noun (the field you have read about)
contrast: The second part rhymes with *bed*, not with *reed* — it is the past participle. *Well-read* is about the reader; a *widely read* book is about the book.

senses.gloss: Having read a lot of books, and knowing a lot because of it.
examples: Her grandfather was a quiet, *well-read* man.
He's *well read* in Russian history.
She's *better read* than anyone I know.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Covering a good range of skills, subjects or experience, not just one.
examples: Colleges look for *well-rounded* applicants.
The program gives students a *well-rounded* education.
This year's class is *better rounded* than last year's.

senses.gloss: Speaking clearly, politely and in an educated way.
examples: He's polite and *well-spoken*.
She was the most *well-spoken* kid on the debate team.
A *well-spoken* young woman showed us around the campus.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Happening at exactly the right moment.
examples: His joke was *well-timed* and broke the tension.
A *well-timed* phone call saved the deal.
The announcement could hardly have been *better timed*.

contrast: *Well-to-do* and *well-off* mean the same thing; *well-to-do* sounds a little older and is more often used before a noun.

senses.gloss: Having plenty of money; comfortably rich.
examples: They live in a *well-to-do* suburb north of the city.
Her family was *well-to-do* but never flashy.
The club draws the more *well-to-do* residents.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

senses.gloss: Used so much that it shows.
examples: He pulled on a pair of *well-worn* jeans.
The stone steps are *well-worn* in the middle.
Her copy of the book is *well worn* and full of notes.

senses.gloss: Of a phrase, a joke or an argument: used too often to be interesting.
examples: The speech was full of *well-worn* phrases.
It's a *well-worn* argument, but it still works.

position: attributive only — *the west side*, *a west wind*
contrast: Before a noun it is the adjective (*west Texas*); after a verb *west* is an adverb (*We drove west*); *the West* is a noun. Capitalize it inside names: *West Virginia*, *the West Coast*.

senses.gloss: In, facing, or coming from the west.
examples: We rented a place on the *west* side of town.
A cold *west* wind blew all afternoon.
The kitchen has a *west* window that gets the evening sun.

contrast: Both words are capitalized, and there is no hyphen. It is also a noun for a person: *She's a West African*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the western part of Africa.
examples: The restaurant serves *West African* food.
*West African* rhythms shaped American blues.
He teaches *West African* history at the university.

ru: идущий на запад, в западном направлении

senses.gloss: Traveling toward the west, or leading west.
examples: There's a wreck on the *westbound* side of the highway.
Take the *westbound* train to Union Station.
All *westbound* flights were delayed by fog.

position: attributive only — *a westerly wind*, *a westerly direction*
contrast: A *westerly* wind blows *from* the west, but a *westerly* course goes *toward* the west. It ends in *-ly* and still is an adjective, not an adverb. The noun *the westerlies* means the winds themselves.

senses.gloss: Coming from the west, or going toward the west.
examples: A steady *westerly* breeze filled the sails.
The storm is moving in a *westerly* direction.
They set off on a *westerly* course toward the islands.

comparison: not gradable — the word is already a superlative

senses.gloss: Farthest to the west.
examples: Alaska has the *westernmost* point in the United States.
They live in the *westernmost* county in the state.
The *westernmost* island is little more than a rock.

position: attributive only — after a verb the word is the adverb *westward*
contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective (*the westward expansion*); after a verb it is an adverb (*We drove westward*). American English uses *westward* for both; British English adds *-s* to the adverb (*westwards*).

senses.gloss: Going or facing toward the west.
examples: The class studies the *westward* expansion of the 1800s.
They made the long *westward* journey by wagon.
A *westward* view of the mountains fills the window.

senses.gloss: Having wheels.
examples: She rolled in a *wheeled* suitcase.
The hospital serves meals from *wheeled* carts.
They loaded the engine onto a *wheeled* platform.

senses.gloss: Breathing — or running — with a rough whistling sound.
examples: The child had a *wheezing* cough all night.
A *wheezing* air conditioner rattled in the window.
He answered in a *wheezing* whisper.

senses.gloss: Playful and a little odd, in a charming way.
examples: The book has *whimsical* illustrations.
Her house is full of *whimsical* little details.
The design is more *whimsical* than practical.

senses.gloss: Changing suddenly and for no good reason.
examples: The rules here are *whimsical* and depend on who's working.
He makes *whimsical* decisions about who gets promoted.

senses.gloss: Complaining in an annoying way, or sounding like it.
examples: Don't be so *whiny* about it.
He has a *whiny* voice that carries across the office.
The kids get *whinier* the longer we stay.

form: compound — *white* + *collar*, from the white shirts office workers wore

senses.gloss: Relating to office work rather than manual work.
examples: The city lost thousands of *white-collar* jobs.
He was convicted of a *white-collar* crime.
*White-collar* employees were told to work from home.

contrast: Russian *седой* is usually *gray-haired* if the hair is still partly dark, and *white-haired* only when it has gone completely white. Note American *gray*, not British *grey*.

senses.gloss: Having white hair.
examples: A *white-haired* woman waved from the porch.
He's *white-haired* now, but the voice is the same.
Two *white-haired* men sat playing chess in the park.

senses.gloss: So hot that the metal glows white.
examples: The steel comes out of the furnace *white-hot*.
He watched the *white-hot* tip of the rod.

senses.gloss: Extremely intense — of anger, attention or success.
examples: She spoke with *white-hot* anger.
The team is on a *white-hot* streak.
The debate has reached a *white-hot* pitch.

ru: с самым строгим вечерним дресс-кодом (фрак и белый галстук)
contrast: *White-tie* is the most formal dress code — tails and a white bow tie; *black-tie* means a tuxedo and is far more common. Without the hyphen it is a noun: *The invitation says white tie*.

senses.gloss: Requiring the most formal evening dress.
examples: It's a *white-tie* dinner at the embassy.
He rented tails for the *white-tie* event.
Very few *white-tie* affairs are left in America.

senses.gloss: Painted white with a thin mixture of lime and water.
examples: A *whitewashed* fence ran along the road.
The cottages are *whitewashed* every spring.

senses.gloss: Cleaned up to hide something shameful.
examples: Critics say the report is *whitewashed*.
The museum gives a *whitewashed* version of the town's history.

position: both — *the whole day* before a noun; *swallow it whole* after a verb
contrast: *Whole* comes after *the*, *my*, *this*: *my whole life*, never *whole my life*. With plural and uncountable nouns use *all*: *all the students*, *all the milk*, not *the whole students*. The *w* is silent — *whole* sounds like *hole* (дыра).

senses.gloss: All of something; entire.
examples: I waited the *whole* day and nobody called.
She ate the *whole* pizza by herself.
The *whole* family came out to the airport.

senses.gloss: In one piece; not cut up or broken.
examples: A snake can swallow an egg *whole*.
Cook the potatoes *whole*, then slice them.

contrast: *Whole-wheat* is made from the whole wheat grain; *whole-grain* is the wider word and covers oats and rye too. British English says *wholemeal*.

senses.gloss: Made with flour that keeps the whole grain.
examples: I'd like *whole-wheat* toast, please.
She only buys *whole-wheat* pasta.
The recipe calls for a cup of *whole-wheat* flour.

senses.gloss: Complete and sincere, with no doubts held back.
examples: The plan has my *wholehearted* support.
She gave a *wholehearted* yes.
His approval was *wholehearted*, which surprised us.

contrast: *Wholesale* is also an adverb (*They buy wholesale*) and a noun. The 'large-scale' sense is nearly always critical: *wholesale destruction*, *wholesale firings*.

senses.gloss: Relating to selling goods in large amounts to stores rather than to shoppers.
examples: We pay the *wholesale* price.
He runs a *wholesale* bakery downtown.
*Wholesale* customers need a tax number.

senses.gloss: Done on a huge scale, and usually without care.
examples: The fire caused *wholesale* destruction downtown.
There were *wholesale* changes in the front office.

senses.gloss: Good for your health, especially of food.
examples: They serve simple, *wholesome* food.
A *wholesome* breakfast beats a donut in the car.
Nothing on that menu looked very *wholesome*.

senses.gloss: Morally good and not offensive.
examples: It's a *wholesome* family movie.
He has a *wholesome*, small-town image.
That video is the most *wholesome* thing on the internet today.

position: attributive only — usually right before a number: *a whopping $40 million*

senses.gloss: Very large — used to stress how big a number or a thing is.
examples: The repair cost a *whopping* twelve hundred dollars.
She won by a *whopping* thirty points.
He pulled a *whopping* trout out of the creek.

contrast: Two syllables, WIK-id, even though it looks like a past tense. In New England *wicked* is also an adverb meaning *very*: *It's wicked cold out.*

senses.gloss: Morally bad; evil — often in stories.
examples: The *wicked* stepmother locks her in the tower.
It was a *wicked* thing to do to an old man.
She plays the *wickedest* villain on TV.

senses.gloss: Very bad, severe or unpleasant.
examples: I've got a *wicked* headache.
A *wicked* storm knocked out the power for two days.

senses.gloss: Excellent or impressive — informal praise.
examples: They have a *wicked* sense of humor.
That's a *wicked* guitar solo.

senses.gloss: Of a camera lens or shot: taking in a much wider view than normal.
examples: He shot the room with a *wide-angle* lens.
A *wide-angle* shot shows the whole stage at once.
The phone has a *wide-angle* camera on the back.

position: predicative only — usually written open after a verb: *I was wide awake*

senses.gloss: Completely awake, not sleepy at all.
examples: It was three in the morning and I was *wide awake*.
The coffee left her *wide awake* until two.
The baby is *wide awake* and ready to play.

senses.gloss: With the eyes wide open in surprise, fear or wonder.
examples: The kids stood *wide-eyed* in front of the shark tank.
A *wide-eyed* toddler watched the parade go by.

senses.gloss: Innocent and easily impressed, because you have seen little of the world.
examples: He came to the city as a *wide-eyed* college kid.
She's not the *wide-eyed* intern she was five years ago.

ru: распахнутый; с непредсказуемым исходом; открытый, просторный
position: both — hyphenated before a noun (*a wide-open field*); written open after a verb (*the door was wide open*)

senses.gloss: Open as far as it will go.
examples: He left the front door *wide open*.
The *wide-open* windows let in all the noise from the street.

senses.gloss: With no clear winner yet, or with no limits.
senses.ru: с непредсказуемым исходом; ничем не ограниченный
examples: The race for governor is *wide open*.
It's a *wide-open* market — anyone can sell there.

senses.gloss: Of land: flat, empty and stretching a long way.
examples: They moved west for the *wide-open* spaces.
The highway runs for hours through *wide-open* country.

senses.gloss: Covering many different subjects, or a large area.
examples: They had a *wide-ranging* conversation about politics and art.
The bill makes *wide-ranging* changes to the tax code.
Her interests are *wide-ranging*, from opera to baseball.

contrast: Americans now usually write it as one word: *a widescreen TV*.

senses.gloss: Made for, or having, a screen that is much wider than it is tall.
examples: The movie was shot in *wide-screen* format.
He bought a *wide-screen* TV for the basement.
The *wide-screen* version keeps the whole picture.

senses.gloss: Happening or found over a large area, or among many people.
examples: The storm caused *widespread* flooding.
There is *widespread* support for the new library.
The practice is more *widespread* than people think.

senses.gloss: Having lost a husband or a wife, and not married again.
examples: He moved in with his *widowed* mother.
She was *widowed* at forty and raised three kids alone.
The program helps *widowed* seniors stay in their homes.

contrast: *In the wild* (в дикой природе) is a noun phrase, and *wildly* is the adverb: *He guessed wildly*.

senses.gloss: Living or growing in nature; not kept or planted by people.
examples: *Wild* horses still roam these hills.
We picked *wild* blackberries along the fence.
The *wildest* parts of the state have no roads at all.

senses.gloss: Not controlled; noisy, crazy or violent.
examples: The crowd went *wild* when the band came out.
It was a *wild* party, and the neighbors called the police.
The wind got *wilder* after midnight.

senses.gloss: Very enthusiastic about something.
senses.ru: в восторге от, без ума от
examples: The kids are *wild* about the new dog.
I'm not *wild* about the color, to be honest.

senses.gloss: Not based on facts; random.
examples: That's a *wild* guess, but it's close.
The rumor is *wild* speculation and nothing more.

senses.gloss: Looking shocked, frightened or half crazy.
examples: A *wild-eyed* man burst into the diner.
She came home *wild-eyed* and out of breath.

senses.gloss: Of a plan or an idea: extreme and completely unrealistic.
examples: Nobody would fund his *wild-eyed* scheme.
The article dismisses the whole thing as *wild-eyed* nonsense.

contrast: American spelling *willful*, British *wilful* with one *l*. In legal English it means 'done on purpose': *willful misconduct*.

senses.gloss: Done on purpose — almost always of something bad.
examples: The judge called it a *willful* violation of the order.
*Willful* ignorance is no excuse.
They were fined for *willful* damage to public property.

senses.gloss: Determined to do what you want, whatever anyone says.
examples: She was a *willful* child who never took no for an answer.
He's too *willful* to follow anyone else's plan.

form: -y from *willow*, the tree with long thin branches

senses.gloss: Tall, slim and graceful.
examples: A *willowy* dancer crossed the stage.
She's *willowy* and quiet, and easy to miss in a crowd.
He remembered her as a *willowy* teenager in a summer dress.

senses.gloss: Of a plant or flower: drooping, usually from lack of water.
examples: She threw out the *wilted* tulips.
The lettuce in the fridge is *wilted*.
A few *wilted* plants sat on the windowsill.

senses.gloss: Of greens: cooked just long enough to go soft.
examples: Serve the steak over *wilted* spinach.
The salad comes with *wilted* greens and bacon.

senses.gloss: Clever at getting what you want, usually by tricks.
examples: The *wily* old lawyer had one more move left.
Coyotes are *wily* enough to live in the suburbs.
He's the *wiliest* negotiator in the building.
